paper_title: Restoring Diversity in Distilled Image and Video Generators by Probing Activations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Distillation turns diffusion-based image and video generators (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Rombach et al., 2022) into fast, few-step models (Salimans & Ho, 2022; Song et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024b;a). But they can reduce the diversity of their outputs: different seeds may produce strikingly similar samples for the same prompt. We explore where in the student diversity disappears. Broadly, there are two solutions to alleviate this problem. (1) Retrain or re-distill the student, either with modified or regularized objective (Xu et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b) or with real data (Chen et al., 2026). (2) Keep the student frozen and intervene at inference, either by optimizing the initial noise (Harrington et al., 2026), by perturbing intermediate features directly in the forward pass (Yadav et al., 2026; Bhat et al., 2026), or by running the teacher for the first step (Gandikota & Bau, 2026). These approaches motivate complementary question: where does the students internal representation cease to preserve the variation present in its teacher, and can that diagnosis guide targeted repair? We start by asking simple question. What would happen to the activations across many seeds when the same prompt is given to teacher and its student? Surprisingly, we found similar pattern emerging in every model we tested, across both image and video families. In particular, at each block, we measure the total activation variance across seeds and its participation ratio, which summarizes how broadly that variance is distributed across directions. We find that in the initial blocks, the students total variance and participation ratio closely match the teachers. However, deeper down, the students total variance equals or exceeds the teachers, but it is restricted to far fewer directions in particular block, resulting in cascaded effect on downstream activations. Interestingly, we show that the collapse in diversity can be attributed to these lost directions and misallocation of variance within single block of the students model. This diagnosis identifies where to supervise the student to recover richer representation. We introduce ReDiverse with two complementary interventions. In ReDiverse-FT, we insert LoRA modules into all layers up to and including the identified block, keeping the base model frozen. We train these modules by regressing the students activation at this block during its first denoising step toward the teachers activation at the corresponding block during its τ -th denoising step. At inference, the LoRA modules are active only during the students first step; subsequent steps use the original student. In ReDiverse-TF, no training is required: we perturb activations at the identified block along teacher principal directions computed once per prompt, with random coefficients scaled by the teachers spread along each direction. The two interventions can be used independently or combined. To summarize, our contributions are threefold: We profile and probe the variance characteristics of distilled students against their teachers, block by block under identical inputs, and show that distillation keeps the total variance but concentrates it into fewer directions at an identifiable block. This locates the collapse, which output metrics cannot, and separates students distilled from the same teacher under different recipes. 2 We introduce ReDiverse to restore variation at the identified block through two complementary interventions: ReDiverse-FT trains LoRA modules in the layers up to and including the identified block to align first-step student activations with later-step teacher activations, while ReDiverseTF perturbs activations along teacher principal directions without training. We evaluate both interventions and their combination on four teacherstudent pairs spanning image (SDXL (Podell et al., 2024), SD3 (Esser et al., 2024)) and video (Wan 2.1 (Wan et al., 2025), MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026)) generators, where ReDiverse restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by user study.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Distillation and Diversity. Distillation compresses iterative diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Rombach et al., 2022; Podell et al., 2024) into few-step students by matching teacher trajectories (Salimans & Ho, 2022), consistency endpoints (Song et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2024), or output distributions via adversarial (Sauer et al., 2024) and distribution-matching (DMD) losses (Wang et al., 2023a; Yin et al., 2024b;a; Luo et al., 2025), recently extended to video transformers (Huang et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026b;a; Shaul et al., 2026; FastVideo Team, 2026; lightx2v, 2026). Because these objectives supervise terminal outputs rather than seed-conditioned activations, distilled students prematurely freeze global structure at the first step (Gandikota & Bau, 2026) and generate near-identical outputs across seeds (Shi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). This collapse has been attributed to mode-seeking reverse KL (Minka et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), adversarial training (Arora et al., 2017), constrained step budgets (Salmona et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2026), or over-guided high-noise targets (Li et al., 2026a). Existing remedies either retrain the student with modified divergences (Xu et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), consistencyDMD hybrids (Zheng et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b), adjusted first-step targets (Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a), or real data (Chen et al., 2026), incurring substantial re-distillation costs and fidelity trade-offs (Li et al., 2026b); or intervene at inference on frozen student via noise optimization (Harrington et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026), teacherstudent hybrid sampling (Gandikota & Bau, 2026), or feature perturbations (Bhat et al., 2026; Yadav et al., 2026). Crucially, neither paradigm localizes where diversity vanishes internally. ReDiverse identifies this breakdown and is agnostic to the distillation recipe. Interpreting diffusion representations. Prior work has shown that the intermediate activations of diffusion model encode attributes of the samples it generates: the U-Net bottleneck forms semantic space (Kwon et al., 2023), whose editing directions can be found from principal components of these features (Haas et al., 2024), the encoders pullback metric (Park et al., 2023), or the low-rank Jacobian of the posterior mean (Chen et al., 2024); all study single model. In distilled students, Gandikota & Bau (2026) find that the directions needed for diversity survive but go unused, and Yadav et al. (2026) inject noise along the students own principal directions, spreading variance it still has. However, we are the first to interpret student and teacher activations together, both to explain why diversity collapses and to remedy it.

sections.title: 3 PROBING DISTILLED DIFFUSION MODELS
sections.content: To identify the internal mechanisms driving diversity collapse, we analyze the representations of distilled diffusion models across network depth and denoising steps. Specifically, we trace the propagation of seed sensitivity by comparing intermediate activations between teacher models and their few-step student counterparts under identical initial latents and conditioning prompts. 3.1 SAME VARIANCE, FEWER DIRECTIONS To characterize the internal representation of block b, we evaluate three geometric quantities derived from the sample covariance matrix Σb across random noise initializations: total variance (TV) Tr(Σb), measuring overall dispersion; the participation ratio PR(Σb) (Gao et al., 2017), quantifying the effective dimensionality spanned by this variance, as eigenvalue-spectrum measures of dimensional collapse do in representation learning (Jing et al., 2022; Garrido et al., 2023); and the concentration ratio Tr(Σb)/PR(Σb), measuring the average variance allocated per active dimension. TV PR 3.2 FEWER DIRECTIONS, LESS DIVERSITY Because downstream layers deterministically map intermediate features to the final output, the directional span of activation variance bounds attainable generative diversity. To test whether the directions lost during distillation govern macroscopic diversity and whether the student can still decode them, we perform activation steering at the collapsed block during the initial denoising step. Specifically, we extract the top principal direction of activation covariance across random noise initializations and perturb intermediate activations along it with increasing strength α, scaled by the empirical standard deviation. Perturbing the teacher along its own principal axis dynamically alters macroscopic attributes, including camera framing, subject pose, and scene composition (Fig. 3a). Crucially, injecting this same teacher direction into the student produces matching structural changes (Fig. 3b), recovering diverse poses and layouts without modifying any student weights. In contrast, steering the student along its own leading axis alters only appearance-level details, such as coat pattern and localized lighting, leaving global geometry invariant (Fig. 3c). This functional asymmetry confirms two key insights: (i) the directions suppressed during distillation are precisely those that dictate structural diversity, and (ii) downstream student layers retain the capacity to decode these modes once restored. Diversity collapse is therefore not an irreversible loss of generative capacity, but geometric misallocation of activation variance. sections.title: 4 REDIVERSE: RESTORING THE LOST DIRECTIONS
sections.content: We introduce ReDiverse, which operationalizes our diagnostic findings through two complementary mechanisms: (i) ReDiverse-FT (Sec. 4.1), targeted fine-tuning framework that regresses student activations onto the teachers at the collapsed block to revive the teachers variance characteristic, and (ii) ReDiverse-TF (Sec. 4.2), training-free inference approach that injects variance along precomputed teacher principal directions to restore the directions the student lost; both hence improve diversity by adjusting the students feature variance characteristic. 4.1 REDIVERSE-FT: DIRECTIONAL ALIGNMENT VIA TARGETED ADAPTATION Feature regression. We implement ReDiverse-FT using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) inserted only into the blocks up to and including the collapsed block ℓ: as these blocks map the initial noise into intermediate representations, adapting only this region enables the student to reproduce the teachers variance characteristic before activations propagate downstream. Downstream layers already retain the capacity to decode diverse structural modes (Sec. 3.2); leaving them frozen preserves native synthesis fidelity without disrupting the rendering pipeline. Because restoring the span redistributes variance across suppressed axes rather than learning new concepts, low-rank adaptation provides an inductive bias that recovers diversity without overfitting (Gan & Isola, 2026). 4.2 REDIVERSE-TF: TRAINING-FREE STOCHASTIC STEERING Because downstream layers can decode the teachers principal directions without parameter updates (Sec. 3.2), we can restore diversity directly at test time by steering intermediate activations along these missing axes. Automatic metrics provide an indirect measure of diversity, so we also evaluate whether people actually perceive the samples as more diverse. This is particularly important for videos, where diversity also involves differences in motion. We therefore ask raters to compare ReDiverse with one method at time, using the same prompt and initial noises, and judge which is more diverse (overall and by aspect), more realistic, and more faithful to the prompt. Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026) performs the same comparisons as an automatic judge (App. J). In the user study  (Fig. 10)  , raters prefer ReDiverse over every 4-step method in diversity, both overall and across all aspects, for both images and videos. They rate ReDiverse on par with the teacher, even slightly higher overall, and also prefer it in prompt following against every method. The VLM judge agrees that ReDiverse is more diverse than the 4-step methods  (Fig. 10)  . More details about the user study are provided in App. J. Ablation Study. Tab. 5 changes one design choice at time on SD3 (full sweeps in App. E). (i) ReDiverse-FT should regress where the teachers directions are lost, at the collapsed block: at an earlier block the student still matches the teacher, so there is less to correct and the gain shrinks, while at later block the adapter also reshapes the blocks that render the image, adding diversity at cost in quality (App. E.1). As the layout is fixed at the first step, regressing at every step or keeping the adapter on after it adds no diversity and lowers prompt alignment (App. E.4). (ii) For ReDiverseTF, what matters is which directions receive variance: the students own directions change appearance but not layout  (Fig. 3)  , single teacher direction is too few because the lost variance is spread over many axes, and random directions of the same scale make samples differ mostly in background texture, at cost in prompt alignment (App. E.7).

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Probing the activations of distilled generators shows that diversity is lost at single collapsed block, where the students features lose the teachers principal directions of variation that the downstream blocks can still render. ReDiverse restores them with short, localized fine-tuning (ReDiverse-FT) or without training (ReDiverse-TF), on images and videos. limitation is that quality still drops at times, most visibly in reward-model scores on images (Tab. 4) and in video realism against the 10 teacher  (Fig. 10)  , as ReDiverse corrects the student after distillation rather than during it. Both variants also assume that the student shares the teachers architecture, as in step distillation; compressed students such as BK-SDM (Kim et al., 2024) would need learned projection between matched blocks, as in FitNets (Romero et al., 2015). In future work, we will use this probing to design new distillation method that keeps the teachers directions at the collapsed block during distillation, so that the student is diverse at the first shot.

sections.title: A MEASURING THE VARIANCE CHARACTERISTIC
sections.content: Our starting question was the following: the teacher generates different-looking outputs for different noises, but the student does not; for the same set of noises it generates similar-looking outputs. Our idea was therefore to look at the internal representations behind these outputs, to understand how different noises end up as different-looking outputs. To measure this, we feed many initial noises through the network, noises that generate different outputs in the teacher and similar outputs in the student, and look at what they produce inside the network. At an internal block each noise gives one activation. We flatten each activation into vector, so from noises we have activation vectors, that is, points in activation space, and we measure the characteristics of the distribution formed by these points. sections.title: D IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: This section provides the implementation details underlying Sec. 5.1. We describe the teacher and student checkpoints, the collapsed block used for each model pair, the training procedure for ReDiverse-FT, and the estimation and injection of directions used by ReDiverse-TF. D.1 BACKBONES AND COLLAPSED BLOCKS We use the publicly released 4-step student checkpoints for all four backbones without modification (Tab. 7). The collapsed block ℓ is selected as described in App. A, and τ denotes the teacher step whose activation is used as the regression target for ReDiverse-FT. Table 7: Checkpoints and collapsed blocks. Teacher and student checkpoints, the teacher sampler, the collapsed block ℓ, the teacher step τ used for the regression target, and the guidance used when computing the target. SDXL SD3-M Wan 2.1 Teacher Student Teacher sampler Collapsed block ℓ Teacher step τ Teacher guidance for the target CFG 8 SDXL-base-1.0 SD3-medium DMD2 (4-step UNet) TDM (LoRA) Euler, 50 steps up0.attn0 7 FM-Euler, 28 steps UniPC, 50 steps block 12 9 CFG 7 block 28 8 CFG 5 Wan2.1-T2V-14B lightx2v (stepand CFG-distilled) MiniMax-H3 MiniMax-H3 lightx2v Turbo FM, 50 steps block 45 16 CFG-distilled D.2 REDIVERSE-FT: ADAPTER TRAINING AND REGRESSION TARGETS Adapter. We insert rank-32 LoRA adapters (α = 32, no dropout, and zero-initialized matrices) into the attention projections (query, key, value, and output) and feed-forward layers up to and including the collapsed block. The adapter is activated only in the students first step; the remaining three steps use the original student. Targets and loss. Given caption and noise sample, the student performs its first step with the adapter enabled, and we extract the activation at the collapsed block. The target is the teacher activation at the same block and step τ . The teacher starts from the same noise and caption, is advanced for τ 1 steps using the corresponding guidance, and is read from its conditional branch at step τ . We minimize plain MSE between the student and teacher activations. For SDXL and Wan 2.1, the loss uses all generated sample tokens. For SD3 and MiniMax-H3, which jointly process prompt and sample tokens, we compute the loss only over image tokens and video tokens, respectively. No additional loss terms are used. Optimization. We train on the first 100 DiffusionDB captions (Wang et al., 2023b), using 16 noise samples per caption for 1,600 captionnoise pairs, disjoint from the evaluation prompts. Each step uses 4 captions and 8 associated noises per caption, giving batch of 32 pairs, for 200 optimization steps. We use AdamW with learning rate 104, weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 10, and constant learning rate. The forward pass uses bf16, while LoRA parameters are maintained in fp32. We retain the final checkpoint and use the same recipe for all four pairs. D.3 REDIVERSE-TF: DIRECTION ESTIMATION AND INJECTION For each evaluation prompt, we run the teacher on = 25 noise samples, independent of the evaluation noise bank, using the conditional branch. We record the activation at step τ (7 for SDXL, 9 for SD3, 8 for Wan 2.1, and 16 for MiniMax-H3), then compute and store the top = 8 directions uk and spreads sk from the Gram matrix following App. B. During inference, each sample independently draws αi,k U[2, 2] and adds (cid:80) αi,kskuk to the students activation at the collapsed block. The perturbation is applied only during the first student step.

sections.title: F EVALUATION PROTOCOL AND METRICS
sections.content: This section describes the evaluation prompts, noise construction, subsets, and metrics used throughout our experiments. Comparisons are paired: all methods are evaluated on the same prompts and the same initial noise samples. F.1 PROMPTS, SEEDS, AND EVALUATION SUBSETS For images, we use the 553 GenEval prompts and generate 100 samples per prompt at 10241024 resolution. For video, we use 300 prompts selected from VBench with fixed quota for each dimension and generate 10 clips per prompt. Wan 2.1 generates 81-frame clips at 832480 and 16 fps, while MiniMax-H3 generates 124-frame clips at 1344768 and 24 fps. For each backbone, we use fixed stored noise bank, so paired methods receive identical initial noise. The coefficients α used by ReDiverse-TF are also generated deterministically, ensuring that ReDiverse-TF (the student carrying the directions, with no adapter) and ReDiverse use identical coefficients. The noises used for direction estimation and the DiffusionDB captions used to train ReDiverse-FT are disjoint from all evaluation prompts and noises. F.2 DIVERSITY METRICS Diversity metrics are computed within each prompt and then averaged across prompts. Except for Vendi, which evaluates the full sample set jointly, and LPIPS, which is learned perceptual distance, the remaining metrics compare pairs of samples from the same prompt using one minus the cosine similarity between their embeddings. Thus, higher values indicate greater diversity. DINO. For images, we use DINOv2-B patch tokens and compare corresponding spatial locations, averaging their cosine distance. This captures differences in layout, pose, and content. For video, we sample 16 frames throughout each clip, including the first and last, and average the corresponding frame distances. DreamSim. DreamSim combines DINO, CLIP, and OpenCLIP features and is fine-tuned to human judgments of visual similarity. It captures perceptual differences in layout, pose, color, and object appearance. LPIPS. LPIPS measures distance between deep VGG features and is sensitive to differences in texture, color, and local structure, including variations that preserve semantic content. TPIPS. TPIPS conditions the visual embedding on the aspect being compared. We use Represent the similarity of the image. for the overall score and Represent the similarity of the image based on X, for the main subject, background scene, lighting and color, and camera viewpoint and framing. TPIPSavg is the mean of the overall and four aspect-specific scores. For video, we sample 8 frames and compute the same comparison frame by frame. Vendi. Vendi measures set-level diversity rather than individual pairwise differences. Given the normalized similarity matrix K, its score is the exponential of the entropy of the eigenvalue distribution of K, reflecting the effective number of distinct samples generated for prompt. For images, we use DINOv2-B CLS features; for video, we use ViCLIP embeddings. F.3 VIDEO-SPECIFIC DIVERSITY Video diversity metrics either compare corresponding frames or represent each clip with single video embedding. V-JEPA 2. We embed 64 frames from each clip using V-JEPA 2 ViT-L and average the resulting tokens. Because the model processes the frames jointly, the metric captures differences in both appearance and motion. 30 ViCLIP. ViCLIP is the videotext model used by VBench. We use 8 frames per clip and compute the distance between clip-level embeddings. ViCLIPdiv therefore captures differences in overall content, while the ViCLIP Vendi score measures the effective number of distinct clips per prompt. Camera trajectory. We estimate camera trajectories with ViPE and express them relative to the first camera position. Each trajectory is resampled to 32 points and normalized by its path length, removing absolute-scale differences. CamTraj is the mean pointwise distance between two normalized trajectories, while CamEnd is the distance between their endpoints. Both are reported after the per-prompt normalization described above: the Cam column of Tab. 4 is the normalized CamTraj and the CamEnd column of Tab. 17 is the normalized CamEnd, so the two columns are not on the same scale and should not be compared with each other. F.4 QUALITY, ALIGNMENT, AND REPORTING Images. CLIP-S measures prompt alignment using the cosine similarity between CLIP (ViT-B/32) image and text embeddings. HPSv2 (version 2.1) and ImageReward are preference models trained on human judgments of generated images; HPSv2 uses CLIP ViT-H/14 backbone. Video. SubjC and BgC are VBench dimensions measuring subject and background consistency across frames using DINO and CLIP features, respectively. ViCLIP-S measures prompt alignment using cosine similarity between the generated clip and prompt embeddings. Reporting. Diversity metrics are computed within each prompt and averaged across prompts, while quality and alignment metrics are averaged over all generated samples. All reported scores are multiplied by 100 except Vendi, ImageReward, and PickScore. In Tab. 4, Teacher and Noise Optimization are reference methods and are not ranked. Among the remaining methods, the best and second-best values are shown in bold and underlined, respectively.

sections.title: G BASELINE REPRODUCTIONS
sections.content: None of the baselines provides checkpoints trained with our teacherstudent pairs, so we reproduced each baseline ourselves. All baselines use the same initial noise bank as the other methods and are evaluated on the full evaluation sets using the protocol described in App. F. G.

sections.title: IMAGE BASELINES
sections.content: Noise Optimization. Noise Optimization (Harrington et al., 2026) keeps the student fixed and optimizes the initial noise at inference time. It optimizes groups of four noise samples using gradient ascent on diversity objective based on DINOv2 features, together with an HPSv2 objective to preserve image quality. We use the authors code and, where applicable, their recommended settings. We use 50 optimization iterations for both SDXL and SD3 to keep the evaluation computationally feasible. For SDXL, the diversity objective is evaluated using DPP with 150 points and the HPSv2 objective uses weight of 3. For SD3, we use 100 DPP points and an HPSv2 weight of 5. Since Noise Optimization directly optimizes DINOv2-based diversity objective, we report it as an optimization-based reference in Tab. 4. DP-DMD. DP-DMD (Wu et al., 2026) distills new 4-step student using DMD and regresses the students first step toward the teachers latent representation at an earlier point in the teachers denoising trajectory. This is intended to preserve the teachers diversity in the distilled student. The released checkpoint is distilled from SD3.5-Medium rather than from our teacher, so we train new students for both SD3 and SDXL from scratch on DiffusionDB prompts. For SD3, we use the authors official implementation. For SDXL, we use our own implementation based on the same training procedure, as the official implementation does not support SDXL. G.2 VIDEO BASELINES DFD. DFD (Chen et al., 2026) post-trains the student with DMD while incorporating real videos into the training process. In half of the updates, the real score is evaluated on noised real video with the same caption instead of on generated sample, encouraging the student to remain closer to the real data distribution. For Wan 2.1, we use the authors implementation with 29k captioned real video clips. MiniMax-H3 is not supported by the released code, so we adapt the method to its student architecture and train it using 2k real video clips. For both models, we first warm up the fake score for 100 iterations and then train DFD for another 100 iterations. We also evaluate several variants of this setup and use the best configuration for DFD in the baseline comparison.

sections.title: J USER STUDY DETAILS
sections.content: Automatic diversity metrics are only proxies and are not designed to capture motion, so we additionally evaluated diversity with human raters. Each trial compares ReDiverse with one baseline, the teacher, the student, or few-step method (DP-DMD (Wu et al., 2026) or Noise Optimization (Harrington et al., 2026) for images; DFD (Chen et al., 2026) for videos), using one prompt and the same initial noises. We use ten prompts per model: generic single-object GenEval prompts for images and VBench scenes/actions for videos, chosen to leave room for diversity. Instruments. Quality and diversity were collected as separate rating jobs  (Fig. 25)  . The quality job asks about realism and prompt following. The diversity job asks about overall diversity, subject, pose and viewpoint, background, and, for videos, motion. The rubric explicitly excludes errors, flicker, and unrelated content from diversity. Raters and aggregation. Each job was rated by 30 or 31 raters, 59 distinct people in total. The A/B order was randomized. No preference counts as half, so 50% represents an even split.
